Date: 2026-10-24 (Europe/Zurich)
CPU: Intel Core i7-11800H @ 2.30 GHz, 16 logical CPUs
Runtime probe: AVX=true, AVX2=true, AVX512=true
Toolchain: go1.27.3 windows/amd64, GOEXPERIMENT=simd, GOAMD64=v1, PGO off
Source commit: 4d8d4ece23bf25513173fa1932b21dab30a7e975

Scope:
  Test the highest-priority remaining SIMD target, relaxStatLengths: calculate
  candidate costs and update both winning costs and their uint16 path lengths.
  All builds include the previously measured AVX2 threshold broadcast in
  firstImprovableLength. Therefore these comparisons isolate the additional
  relaxation changes, not the gain over the original scalar compressor.
  Production Go sources are unchanged; complete candidate patches are retained.

Fresh baseline profile:
  baseline-profile.pb.gz and baseline-profile.txt contain a new profile of the
  broadcast baseline on this computer, aggregated across all six default gzip
  corpora (four timed operations each plus calibration and round-trip checks).
  The profiling binary uses the source commit's original test harness.
  Command, run from the working repository root:
    <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkPureGoGzip$ -test.benchtime=4x -test.count=1 -test.cpu=1 -test.cpuprofile=<profile>
    go tool pprof -top -nodecount=30 <binary> <profile>
  Duration 15.72 s, sampled CPU time 15.36 s. Flat sample shares:
    firstImprovableLength: 30.53%
    relaxStatLengths: 22.01%
    getBestLengthsStat: 15.49%
    storeRunsFromSublen: 3.58%
    getMatch: 3.52%
  profile-bench.txt is a profiled run, not part of the timing comparison.

Builds:
  baseline: AVX2 broadcast prototype plus original scalar relaxStatLengths.
  scalar-writes: calculate and compare four float64 costs with AVX2-enabled
    BroadcastFloat64x4 and IfElse; extract the four-bit improvement mask and
    write winning uint16 lengths individually. Skip stores if no lane improves.
    Ranges shorter than four entries call the original scalar helper.
  packed-writes: calculate eight costs in two four-lane vectors. Convert the
    comparison masks to integer vectors, use VPERMD to select one 32-bit word
    per 64-bit mask, and VPACKSSDW to pack eight 16-bit masks. Combine the new
    indices and old lengths using AND/ANDNOT/OR, then store eight lengths.
    Ranges shorter than eight entries call the original scalar helper.
  inline-scalar: refinement of scalar-writes that keeps the scalar fallback
    loop inside the same function, avoiding a second call for short ranges.
  All SIMD paths require X86.AVX2(), preserve strictly-less comparisons, use
  overlapping full-vector tails, and execute VZEROUPPER before returning.
  Assembly snapshots document the emitted instructions. The tested operations
  require AVX/AVX2, not AVX-512, although this CPU also reports AVX-512 support.

Source and reproduction:
  Create separate source trees at the commit above.
  For baseline, apply ../avx2-broadcast/candidate.patch.
  For each candidate, apply its matching patch from this directory instead;
    each complete patch already includes the broadcast change.
  Copy relax_measurement_test.go.txt and measurement_cpu_test.go.txt into every
    tree, dropping the .txt suffix. These are identical test/benchmark harnesses.
  Build with GOEXPERIMENT=simd GOAMD64=v1 go test -c -pgo=off -o <binary>.
  Run binaries from the working repository root to use its CRLF fixtures.
  Corpus construction, seeded random input, fixture hashes and input sizes
    are unchanged from ../metadata.txt and its input/fixture digest files.
  GOFLAGS, GODEBUG and GOMAXPROCS unset during timing; -test.cpu=1 sets one Go CPU.
  No explicit CPU affinity. No tests, builds, profiling, or other benchmarks
    run concurrently with the timing runs. No samples are discarded.

Initial compression comparison:
  <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkPureGoGzip$ -test.benchtime=2x -test.count=1 -test.cpu=1
  Six samples per build, two timed compressions plus Go's untimed calibration
  per invocation. Default gzip, 15 iterations, block splitting enabled.
  All six permutations, recorded with UTC timestamps in run-order.txt:
    baseline, scalar-writes, packed-writes
    packed-writes, scalar-writes, baseline
    scalar-writes, packed-writes, baseline
    baseline, packed-writes, scalar-writes
    packed-writes, baseline, scalar-writes
    scalar-writes, baseline, packed-writes
  Medians are the mean of the third and fourth sorted samples.

Initial median times (milliseconds):
Corpus             Baseline  Scalar writes  Saved       Packed writes  Saved
tiny-text             8.03       8.25        -2.7%           8.13       -1.2%
mixed-256k         1479.59    1387.86         6.2%        1499.62       -1.4%
web-assets-256k     436.66     428.22         1.9%         431.93        1.1%
records-logs-256k   509.79     499.04         2.1%         506.29        0.7%
real-files-256k     441.96     435.40         1.5%         440.47        0.3%
random-256k         122.81     123.02        -0.2%         123.08       -0.2%
  Saved = 100 * (1 - median candidate / median baseline), unrounded values.
  Every scalar-writes mixed-256k sample is faster (1375.53-1412.41 ms) than
  every baseline sample (1468.88-1485.75 ms). Other ranges overlap.
  Packing all length writes is not an end-to-end win in this initial run.

    baseline, inline-scalar, scalar-writes

Conclusion:
  Scalar length writes are the promising candidate: their mixed-corpus gain
  repeats at 6.2% and 6.0%, with every candidate sample faster than every
  baseline sample in both runs. Inline scalar fallback reaches 6.6% in the
  confirmation run, but its range overlaps the simpler candidate's range;
  there is no convincing evidence that the extra duplicated loop is better.
  Both variants retain a roughly 1.4% tiny-text regression in the confirmation
  medians. All non-mixed corpus ranges overlap the baseline, so smaller gains
  and regressions remain uncertain. No confidence intervals are claimed.
  Retain scalar-writes.patch as the simplest follow-up candidate. Do not promote
  packed writes based on their synthetic gains. Production remains unchanged.
  These are incremental comparisons against the AVX2 broadcast baseline;
  do not combine them arithmetically with earlier runs against main or AVX.
  The older i7-3610QM has no AVX2 and would use the scalar relaxation fallback;
  these candidates have not been measured on that computer.

Focused benchmarks (*-micro.txt):
  <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkRelaxStatLengths$ -test.benchtime=100ms -test.count=1 -test.cpu=1
  Six rounds in the same six build-order permutations, after compression timing.
  Five range sizes (4, 8, 16, 64, 256) and three improvement patterns (none,
  alternating half, all). Costs are reset by a copy before EVERY invocation,
  including in the timed section for all builds, so the hit pattern stays fixed.
  These timings include reset overhead and are not isolated instruction latency.

Selected median times (nanoseconds):
Range/pattern       Baseline  Scalar writes  Packed writes
4/half                 6.9225      8.7045         7.4530
8/all                 10.830      10.195         14.020
16/all                19.290      14.505         16.240
64/half               44.555      49.110         33.665
256/none             324.550     103.500        131.050
256/all              333.500     172.600        131.500
  Packed writes are effective on long synthetic ranges, but setup and mask
  conversion cost hurt short ranges. The workload mix matters more than the
  largest microbenchmark speedup. The inline-scalar refinement addresses an
  additional short-range helper call in the simpler candidate.

Correctness and fallback coverage:
  *-checks.txt records pre-benchmark boundary and golden-output checks.
  TestRelaxationExperimentBoundaries checks every legal range size, offsets
    0-7, NaNs (including payload preservation), infinities, signed zero, ties,
    and exact cost bits/lengths against an independent scalar reference.
  TestRelaxationExperimentMasks checks all 256 eight-lane improvement masks
    at offsets 0-7 and lengths 1-24, including overlapping tails. Costs and
    lengths outside the selected range must remain unchanged.
  Each compression benchmark performs a gzip round-trip check.
  *-digests.txt records 18 hashes per build: all six corpora in default/fast
    gzip plus the generated fixture in gzip/zlib/deflate with both profiles.
    They are compared with the existing i7-11800H digests, which also match
    the other computer's output. Allocation bytes and counts are compared too.
  Full suites run for every candidate with GOEXPERIMENT=simd, with the
    experiment unset, and with the relaxation fallback forced in a temporary
    copy by replacing !archsimd.X86.AVX2() with true. See validation.txt.
    This forces the new relaxation fallback only; the scanner is unchanged.
  Windows Go 1.27.3 ignores GODEBUG CPU overrides, so those flags are not used
    as evidence of fallback coverage. Forced source checks do not emulate
    hardware lacking AVX2.
